planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Ventura is a Four Winds Growers introduction believed to be a Meyer-lemon-type seedling selection, valued for cold hardiness roughly comparable to or exceeding Improved Meyer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun, watering deeply and regularly during the growing season. Ventura lemon produces medium-sized, thin-skinned, juicy fruit with a mild, less acidic flavor similar to Meyer lemon, borne nearly year-round on a compact, thornless tree well suited to patio containers. Mature trees tolerate brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s F better than standard Eureka or Lisbon lemon, though young trees should still be protected with frost cloth during hard freezes. Fertilize with a citrus-specific balanced fertilizer three times annually and watch for iron and zinc deficiencies in alkaline soils.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ujukitsu is a traditional Japanese citrus of uncertain hybrid origin (probably a natural mandarin-pomelo cross) grown mainly as a specialty and collector variety, with fruit intermediate in size between a mandarin and a grapefruit.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and regularly through the growing season. Ujukitsu bears large, pale orange-yellow fruit with a loose, easy-peeling rind and a mild, semi-sour flavor milder than a true orange but more assertive than a sweet mandarin, ripening in mid-to-late winter. It is grown chiefly in specialty and heirloom citrus collections rather than commercial production, and performs best in the warmer parts of zone 9 and in zones 10-11 where hard freezes are rare. Fertilize with a citrus-specific balanced fertilizer three times annually.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost danger passes, in well-drained soil in full sun; Aoshima is a bud-sport strain of Owari satsuma selected in Japan for a later ripening window and slightly larger, deeper-colored fruit.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and water and feed regularly through the growing season to size up the crop. Aoshima ripens later than standard Owari, typically in December, with seedless, easy-peeling mandarins that are slightly larger and deeper orange than the base variety, holding well on the tree without excessive puffiness. Mature, dormant trees tolerate brief drops to roughly 15-20F, making Aoshima suitable for zone 8b-9a dooryard citrus, though young trees should be covered during hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost danger passes, in well-drained soil in full sun; Kuno Wase is an early-ripening bud-sport strain of Owari satsuma popular with Gulf Coast home growers for delivering a ripe crop before the first hard freezes of late fall.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and regularly through the growing season. Kuno Wase ripens in October, among the earliest of the satsuma strains, with small-to-medium, seedless, loose-skinned mandarins of good sweet-tart flavor that reliably mature before the first hard freeze in Gulf Coast and lower-South climates. Mature, dormant trees tolerate brief drops to roughly 15-20F; protect young trees with frost cloth for the first two or three winters until the root system matures.
